root.claim: One deterministic multitape Turing machine multiplies $n$-bit integers exactly in $O(n(\lg n)^{1-\kappa})$ time with $\kappa=2^{-182}$, refuting the $n\log n$ optimality conjecture in this model.
root.method: Reduce the product to a convolution of short digits evaluated by Fourier transforms, speed up the two costly ingredients (moving data between addresses, and butterfly arithmetic) by a power of a block size using one recursive saving, and total every cost term.

motivation.text: A plain transform scans $\Theta(n)$ bits at each of $\Theta(\log n)$ levels, which already costs $n\log n$, so both the data movement and the arithmetic must be made cheaper than a full scan per level.

quote.quote:
Scanning an array of $\Theta(n)$ stored bits at each of
$\Theta(\log n)$ transform levels already costs $\Theta(n\log n)$.
We therefore need savings in both movement and arithmetic.

root.salient: The saving $\kappa=2^{-182}$ is astronomically small, yet it is a genuine power of $\log n$: the running time is $o(n\log n)$ through all input lengths, which refutes an eventual $\Omega(n\log n)$ lower bound.

children.claim: All later procedures are built from linear-time tape scans: splitting and merging on a digit, distributing whole rows among a fixed number of streams, and shifting a target field by an offset computed from earlier fields.
children.method: State the elementary scans once, each costing $O(V)$ on a fixed number of tapes, so later sections can cite them.

motivation.text: The later tape procedures only use a few elementary scans, so they are proved once up front.

quote.quote:
The present section supplies
the elementary scans it uses.

children.claim: Moving or permuting digit values at specified radix positions, splitting on a digit and merging after a pointwise map, and splitting whole rows cyclically into a fixed number of streams each take $O(V)$ steps on an array of volume $V$.

quote.quote:
Each of the following operations on an array of
volume $V$ takes $O(V)$ steps on a fixed number of one-dimensional tapes:

children.claim: Adding to a later field $y\in[Q]$, $Q=q^b$, an offset computed from earlier control fields, or multiplying it by a rational unit, costs $O(V)$ by splitting blocks and re-merging them.

quote.quote:
An update
\[
 y\longmapsto y+a(\text{controls})\pmod Q
\]
costs $O(V)$ if the offset can be prepared in $b^{O(1)}$ time from the
fixed number of control values.

children.claim: Two disjoint equal-width bit chunks of $u$ bits in an address array of volume $V$ can be interchanged in $O(Vu^\tau)$ steps for a fixed $\tau<1$, by XOR combinations whose final effect is an exact permutation.
children.method: First interchange chunks whose width is a power of $m$ and which have enough rows (the key construction), then remove those restrictions by taking rows from a few high digits of the chunks, cutting the remaining width into base-$m$ pieces, and padding binary chunks to the working radix.

motivation.text: The fast operation is proved only for power widths with enough rows; a few high digits of the array supply the rows and their movement is cheaper than the final bound.

quote.quote:
We have proved the fast operation for power widths with enough rows.
Rows for a general array can be supplied by a few of its own high digits.
Their movement will cost less than the final bound.

children.salient: The cost per stored bit is only $u^\tau$ with $\tau=1-2^{-50}$, a power of the chunk width below the first power, although the exponent is barely under one.

children.claim: Two address chunks of $e=m^k$ radix-$q$ digits can be interchanged in $O(Ve^\tau)$ time by running the bit network on $W$ cyclic role streams, with one smaller interchange per unit of edge rank.
children.method: Run the exchange network on arrays: give each vertex an address-shear frame, split the rows among the $W$ roles so every gate acts pointwise, make each edge cost one smaller interchange per unit of its rank, and solve the resulting recurrence.

motivation.text: Each recursive call handles a stream of volume $V/W$ at width $e/m$, so after dividing by volume the width multiplies the cost by $s/W$, which is less than the factor $m$ in the width itself.

quote.quote:
After dividing cost by volume, multiplying the parameter by $m$
increases the recursive contribution by $s/W<m$. This strict inequality
is the source of the power saving.

children.salient: The final effect is an exact permutation of the stored bits, although the intermediate steps are XOR combinations of data, and it is correct whatever the initial contents of the scratch roles.

adds.name: wire count
adds.meaning: The number of wires (roles) of the fixed bit network.

adds.name: label dimension
adds.meaning: The dimension of the label space, equal to the number of digit fields into which each chunk is cut.

adds.name: total edge rank
adds.meaning: The sum of the ranks of all edge matrices, which is the number of smaller interchanges one run of the network needs.

adds.name: chunk width
adds.meaning: The number of radix-q digits in each of the two chunks being interchanged, a power of m.

adds.name: saving exponent
adds.meaning: A fixed exponent below one with s/W < m^tau, giving cost O(V e^tau).

children.claim: A fixed network of $W$ wires built from three-element subsets, run in three stages, sends $(X_a,Y_a)$ to $(-Y_a,X_a)$ and returns every scratch wire to its arbitrary initial value.
children.method: In each stage add the source bank to the target bank through gather/scatter terms whose coefficients depend on intersection size, cancel the unwanted coefficients with side wires, and wrap this in subtract-and-restore steps that cancel the unknown scratch contents; three stages then give the signed exchange.

motivation.text: The first rows of the schedule remove the effect of the unknown scratch values, the middle rows add the source's effect to the target, and the last rows put the scratch values back.

quote.quote:
The first two rows of
the following schedule remove the effect of the old scratch values;
the next four introduce the source values and add their effect to the
target; the last two restore the scratch values.

children.salient: The exchange works for arbitrary initial values of every auxiliary wire: the first rows subtract the effect of whatever the scratch wires held, and the last rows restore them.

children.claim: For any initial values $a,c$ of the scratch wires, the net change of the targets in one invocation is $(\mathcal J\mathcal V+\mathcal R\mathcal G)x$ (side injection after copy, scatter after gather), independent of $a$ and $c$.

quote.quote:
The net target change is
$(\mathcal J\mathcal V+\mathcal R\mathcal G)x$, independently of
$a,c$.

children.claim: The side injection cancels the unwanted central coefficients (intersection one in the bit case), so the net map is $y\gets y+x$.

quote.quote:
In the bit case, the central coefficient from $x_T$ to $y_S$ is
$|S\cap T|\bmod2$.  The side contribution cancels exactly the
intersection-one cases; distinct triples with intersection zero or two
already have coefficient zero, and the self coefficient is one.

children.claim: Forward, inverse-forward and forward stages send $(x,y)$ to $(x,y+x)$, then $(-y,y+x)$, then $(-y,x)$.

quote.quote:
Starting from $(x,y)$, the three stages give
$(x,y+x)$, then $(-y,y+x)$, then $(-y,x)$.

children.method: Maintain the invariant that the stored array equals the frame applied to the logical array, using linearity at every gate, and read off the operator on each route from the endpoint frames.

motivation.text: Once the endpoint frames fix what each route does, the intermediate frames are free to be chosen so that each edge is cheap.

quote.quote:
Once the scalar routing is fixed,
the endpoint frames determine the array operator on each route; the
intermediate frames can then be chosen to make each edge change inexpensive.

children.salient: Only the two endpoint frames survive on each route, and they act on every role, scratch roles included; every intermediate frame cancels.

children.claim: Because the gate is $R$-linear, $G(D_vg_1,\ldots,D_vg_t)=D_vG(g_1,\ldots,g_t)$, so the invariant continues to the sinks and the implemented operator is $D_{\rm out}\mathsf S_\Omega D_{\rm in}^{-1}$.

children.claim: For a signed role permutation, the route from input role $w$ to output role $\rho(w)$ with sign $\varepsilon_w$ applies $\varepsilon_wD_{\mathrm{sink}(\rho(w))}D_{\mathrm{source}(w)}^{-1}$, on auxiliary roles too.

quote.quote:
In particular, if the scalar network is a signed role permutation that
sends input role $w$ to output role $\rho(w)$ with scalar sign
$\varepsilon_w$, that route applies
$\varepsilon_wD_{\mathrm{sink}(\rho(w))}
D_{\mathrm{source}(w)}^{-1}$ to its input array.

children.claim: In the bit network the total rank $s$ of all edge changes $M_{\mathrm{head}(e)}-M_{\mathrm{tail}(e)}$ is strictly less than $Wm$, the endpoint matrices differ by the identity on every role, and consequently $s/W<m^\tau$ for $\tau=1-2^{-50}$.
children.method: Take each edge matrix to be a difference of orthogonal projections onto the nested labels, so its rank is the dimension change; add up dimension changes over the network (plus one extra rank per source) and compare with $Wm$.

motivation.text: The saving comes from the small total dimension lost on decreasing edges.

quote.quote:
The saving will come from keeping the total dimension lost on decreasing
edges small relative to $N$.

children.salient: The total rank is below $Wm$ by a margin of only about $10^{-14}$ in relative terms, yet any strict deficit suffices to give a power saving $m^	au$ with $	au<1$; the deficit comes from the few decreasing edges and the unit-rank sources.

children.claim: Attaching nested nondegenerate subspaces of the $m$-dimensional space $F^{\otimes 3}$ to gates and terminals makes each edge's orthogonal residual have dimension equal to the number of smaller operations the edge needs; only the central-wire edges from time 3 to time 4 decrease, with total loss $L<N/2$.
children.method: Build labels from indicator vectors of three-element subsets (neighbouring subsets give orthogonal vectors), tensor them over the three stages, and read every edge's residual dimension from a table.

motivation.text: The intermediate labels are chosen so that every change of frame is as small as possible.

quote.quote:
The scalar network already has the required signed exchange. We now
choose its intermediate labels to make the changes of frame inexpensive.

children.salient: Only one kind of edge, the return of a central wire from time 3 to time 4, ever loses dimension, and it loses exactly $h$; the total loss is a fixed fraction (100/539) of the source dimension $N$, well under one half.

children.claim: Every triple line is nondegenerate and neighbouring triple lines are orthogonal, in the label field of either construction.

quote.quote:
Thus every triple line is nondegenerate, and neighboring triple lines
are orthogonal, in the label field belonging to either construction.

children.claim: Every edge joins comparable nondegenerate labels, and the only decreasing edges are the central-wire edges from time 3 to time 4, each losing dimension $h$.

quote.quote:
Every edge joins comparable nondegenerate labels.  The only decreasing
edges are the central-wire edges from time 3 to time 4; their dimension
loss is $h$.

children.claim: Signed dimension changes telescope at each gate to $Wm-2N$, so the absolute changes sum to $Wm-2N+2L$ where $L=Ich$ is the loss on decreasing edges.

quote.quote:
The signed sum of dimension changes telescopes at every gate: each
touched wire has one incoming and one outgoing incidence with the same
gate label.  The sum of source dimensions is $N$, while the sum of
sink dimensions is $Wm-N$.  The signed increase is therefore $Wm-2N$.
There are $Ic$ decreasing edges, each of loss $h$; replacing signed
changes by absolute changes adds $2L$.

children.claim: The loss ratios are $L_{\rm b}/N=100/539$ and $L_{\rm c}/N=101/539$, both smaller than $1/2$.

quote.quote:
The loss ratios have the exact values
\[
 \frac{L_{\rm b}}{N}=\frac{100}{539},\qquad
 \frac{L_{\rm c}}{N}=\frac{101}{539}.
\]
In particular, both are smaller than $1/2$.

children.claim: For nested nondegenerate labels $U\subset V$, the matrix $P_V-P_U$ has rank $\dim V-\dim U$, so an edge's rank equals its dimension change.

quote.quote:
For $U\subset V$ nondegenerate,
$P_V-P_U$ is the identity on $V\cap U^\perp$ and zero on its
orthogonal complement.  Its rank is $\dim V-\dim U$; reversing the
edge negates the matrix without changing its rank.

children.claim: Apart from the $N$ negative source projections, edge ranks equal dimension changes, so the rank sum is $s=Wm-N+2L$ with deficit $N-2L>0$ below $Wm$.

quote.quote:
Lemma~\ref{lem:motif-residuals} consequently gives the stated rank sum.
Its deficit from $W_{\rm b}m$ is $N-2L_{\rm b}>0$.

children.claim: For an input $X_a$ the endpoint difference is $P_{U_a^\perp}-(-P_{U_a})=I_m$; every other role has source matrix $0$ and sink matrix $I_m$.

quote.quote:
For an input $X_a$ the endpoint difference is
$P_{U_a^\perp}-(-P_{U_a})=I_m$.  Every other role has zero source
matrix and identity sink matrix.  This proves the interface.

children.claim: The relative deficit exceeds $20\cdot2^{-50}$, so $m^{1-2^{-50}}>m(1-\eta)$ and hence $s/W<m^\tau$ with $\tau=1-2^{-50}$.

quote.quote:
Consequently
\[
 \frac{s_{\rm b}}{W_{\rm b}}<m^\tau,
 \qquad \frac{s_{\rm c}}{W_{\rm c}}<m^\sigma,
 \qquad 0<\tau=\sigma<1.

children.claim: Every rational $m\times m$ matrix $A$ of rank $a$ factors as $E_1\Pi E_2$ with $E_1,E_2$ invertible lower triangular and $\Pi$ a partial permutation matrix with exactly $a$ ones.
children.method: Eliminate from the topmost nonzero row and its rightmost nonzero entry, using lower-triangular column operations to clear its row and lower-triangular row operations to clear its column, then repeat on the remaining active indices.

motivation.text: Lower-triangular changes of coordinates are the ones that can be done in the direction in which controlled shifts work (later field updated from earlier fields).

quote.quote:
Lemma~\ref{lem:ordered-affine-streams} updates a later field using
earlier fields in linear time.  Lower triangular changes of coordinates
can be performed entirely in this direction.

children.claim: Pick the topmost nonzero row and its rightmost nonzero entry as pivot, clear the entries to its left and below by lower-triangular elementary matrices, and scale the pivot to one.

quote.quote:
Otherwise choose the topmost
nonzero row and its rightmost nonzero entry.  Use that pivot column to
clear entries to its left by right multiplication by lower triangular
elementary matrices.  There are no nonzero entries to its right in the
pivot row.  Clear entries below the pivot by left multiplication by
lower triangular elementary matrices, and scale the pivot to one.

children.claim: Each step isolates a rank-one block, so the final partial permutation matrix has exactly $a$ ones.

quote.quote:
Each step isolates a rank-one block and leaves the
remaining rank in the active submatrix.  Thus the final partial
permutation matrix has exactly $a$ ones.

children.claim: For a rational $m\times m$ matrix $A$ of rank $a$ and fields over $\mathbb Z/q^b\mathbb Z$, the map $(H,D)\mapsto(H+AD,D)$ is performed with exactly $a$ interchanges of $b$-digit fields plus $O(V)$ further work.
children.method: Conjugate by the triangular factors of $A=E_1\Pi E_2$, each costing only linear time, so that only the partial permutation $\Pi$ remains, and realise each one of $\Pi$ as $H_i\leftarrow H_i+D_j$ by one interchange between two cheap controlled updates.

motivation.text: Triangular factors can be applied with controlled shifts in linear time, so the only expensive operations left are interchanges, one per one in $\Pi$, which is why the number of interchanges equals the rank.

children.claim: A lower-triangular transformation of the $H$ fields, or of the $D$ fields, costs $O(V)$ by updating coordinates in descending physical order.

quote.quote:
A lower triangular transformation of $H$, or of $D$, costs $O(V)$:
update coordinates in descending physical order.

children.claim: For $A=E_1\Pi E_2$, transform $D$ by $E_2$ and $H$ by $E_1^{-1}$, add $\Pi D$ to $H$, then transform $H$ by $E_1$ and $D$ by $E_2^{-1}$.

quote.quote:
For $A=E_1\Pi E_2$, first transform $D$ by $E_2$ and $H$ by $E_1^{-1}$,
then add $\Pi D$ to $H$, and finally transform $H$ by $E_1$ and $D$ by
$E_2^{-1}$.

children.claim: Each one of $\Pi$ becomes $H_i\leftarrow H_i+D_j$ via $D_j\leftarrow D_j+H_i$, an interchange of $H_i$ and $D_j$, and $D_j\leftarrow H_i-D_j$, using just one interchange.

quote.quote:
Implement it by
\[
 D_j\leftarrow D_j+H_i,\qquad
 (H_i,D_j)\leftarrow(D_j,H_i),\qquad
 D_j\leftarrow H_i-D_j.
\]
The first and last updates target a later field controlled by an earlier
field.  On an initial pair $(h,d)$ this sequence yields $(h+d,d)$.
It uses just one interchange.

children.claim: There are $a$ ones, so exactly $a$ interchanges are needed.

quote.quote:
There are $a$ ones, which proves the
claim.  In particular, the number of recursive calls is the rational
rank $a$; temporary tapes used for the other operations do not multiply
that count.

children.claim: Splitting whole rows cyclically into $W$ role streams gives streams of identical shape, each of logical volume $V/W$, on which every gate acts pointwise.

quote.quote:
Split whole rows cyclically into $W$ role streams within each prefix
preceding the row field.  Write the original row number as
$r=Wg+(w-1)$ with $1\le w\le W$; stream $w$ has row number $g$.
These streams have exactly the same remaining shape, including the
full ranges of $H$ and $D$.  Each has
logical volume $V/W$

children.claim: Applying the shear $\Phi_{A_e}$ on every edge and the gates pointwise, the endpoint identity makes the physical output of role $\rho(w)$ equal to $\Phi_{I_m}f_w$, that is the shear $H\leftarrow H+D$ on every row, scratch rows included.

quote.quote:
Thus its physical output satisfies
\[
 f'_{\rho(w)}
 =\Phi_{M_{\mathrm{out}(\rho(w))}}
   \Phi_{-M_{\mathrm{in}(w)}}f_w
 =\Phi_{I_m}f_w,
\]
by~\eqref{eq:finite-shear-contract}.

children.claim: Three updates $D\leftarrow D-H$, $H\leftarrow H+D$ (through the network) and $D\leftarrow H-D$ send $(H,D)$ to $(D,H)$; only the middle shear uses the network.

quote.quote:
To interchange the two full chunks, perform
\[
 D\leftarrow D-H,\qquad H\leftarrow H+D,\qquad D\leftarrow H-D,
\]
componentwise.  Only the middle shear uses the circuit.  The other two
updates target the later group and have linear cost.  The transformation
sends $(H,D)$ to $(D,H)$.

children.claim: With $F_k$ the time per unit volume at width $e=m^k$, one run of the network makes $s$ smaller interchanges, each on a stream of volume $V/W$, so $F_k\le(s/W)F_{k-1}+O(1)$ and, since $s/W<m^\tau$, $F_k=O(e^\tau)$.
children.method: Count the recursive calls (one per unit of edge rank, $s$ in all), divide by the current volume to get the factor $s/W$ per level, and sum the resulting geometric series over the $k=\log_m e$ levels.

motivation.text: Each child call works on only $1/W$ of the parent's volume, so dividing the total cost by the parent's volume gives the factor $s/W$; because this factor is below $m^\tau$, the geometric sum stays a power of the width below the first.

children.salient: Multiplying the chunk width by $m$ multiplies the normalised cost by only $s/W<m$, so the cost per bit grows like $e^\tau$ with $\tau<1$ instead of linearly in $e$; this strict inequality is the whole source of the power saving.

children.claim: The number of recursive calls is the sum of the edge ranks, exactly $s$, and each acts on one role stream of volume $V/W$.

quote.quote:
The number of recursive calls is the sum of the edge ranks, exactly $s$.
Each acts on one role stream of volume $V/W$, retaining all other
fields as spectators.

children.claim: If $F_k$ bounds time divided by logical volume, then $F_0=O(1)$ and $F_k\le(s/W)F_{k-1}+O(1)$.

quote.quote: F_0=O(1),\qquad F_k\le(s/W)F_{k-1}+O(1).

children.claim: For $a=s/W<m^\tau$ the geometric sum $\sum_{j=0}^ka^j$ is $O(m^{k\tau})$, hence $F_k=O(e^\tau)$.

quote.quote:
For $a=s/W<m^\tau$ the geometric sum
$\sum_{j=0}^k a^j$ is $O(m^{k\tau})$.  If $a\le1$, the sum is at
most $k+1=O(m^{k\tau})$; if $a>1$, it is $O(a^k)$.
Hence $F_k=O(e^\tau)$.

children.claim: On a fixed number of tapes the $W-1$ inactive role streams are parked on a stack before a recursive call, so each node pays only an extra $O(V)$ and temporary storage is not substituted for volume in the factor $s/W$.

quote.quote:
Before a recursive call, append the $W-1$ inactive role streams to the
parking stack in a fixed order, with separators.  Copy the active stream
to the child I/O area, and erase the parent role tapes while traversing
their current contents.

children.claim: Supply the $W^k$ rows the power-width call needs by interchanging the top $\rho=O(\log e)$ digits of the two chunks one pair at a time, then padding to a multiple of $W^k$ rows.

quote.quote:
Write each chunk as its top $\rho$ digits followed by its remaining
digits, denoted $h^+,h^-$ and $d^+,d^-$, respectively.  Interchange
the corresponding high digits one pair at a time.

children.claim: Writing the remaining width in base $m$, cut each chunk into corresponding pieces of widths $m^j$ and interchange each pair by the power-width procedure.

quote.quote:
Partition each remaining chunk into corresponding consecutive pieces,
with $a_j$ pieces of width $m^j$.  Apply
Proposition~\ref{prop:power-interchange} to each corresponding pair.

children.claim: The pieces cost $O(V)\sum_ja_jm^{j\tau}=O(Ve^\tau)$ in total, using $a_j<m$ and $m^k<me$.

quote.quote:
The sum of the costs is bounded by
\[
 O(V)\sum_j a_jm^{j\tau}=O(Ve^\tau).

children.claim: For binary chunks of $u$ bits, pad each range to $[q^e]$ with $q^e\ge2^u$, interchange, and scan the padding away; since $e=O(u)$ the bound is $O(Vu^\tau)$.

quote.quote:
Finally, for binary chunks let $e$ be the least integer with
$q^e\ge2^u$.  Pad each of the two chunk ranges numerically from $[2^u]$
to $[q^e]$, putting zero in an entry if either chunk coordinate is
invalid.  The increase in volume is less than $q^2$, a fixed factor.
The padding is a nested scan through consecutive valid and invalid
intervals, with their lengths prepared from the shape.  It costs $O(V)$
with a constant depending on $q$.  Lexicographic radix-$q$ order of
$[q^e]$ is its numerical order, just as binary order of $[2^u]$ is its
numerical order.  Padding therefore preserves the order of the existing
entries without converting the digits of every address.
The completed interchange preserves the set on which both chunk
coordinates lie below $2^u$.  Scan away the other entries to recover the
desired binary array.  Since $e=O(u)$ for fixed $q$, the bound is
$O(Vu^\tau)$.

children.claim: Applying $H_0(u,v)=((u+v)/2,(u-v)/2)$ to one selected bit in each of $D\le d$ address chunks of $K$ bits, on records of $r$ complex coefficients, costs $O(Vd^{\lambda'})$ for a fixed $\lambda'<1$, instead of $D$ whole-array passes, and is exact up to one final truncation.
children.method: Rerun the rank-saving recursion with the complex phase network: express the tensor product of $H_0$ through the kernel $C$, whose frame change on an edge is one translation kernel per residual basis vector, so each edge becomes smaller layers on slots of fewer chunks, with the binary basis changes done by packed whole-chunk moves.

motivation.text: Phase frames express a tensor product of the kernel $C$ through smaller groups of selected bits separated by binary basis changes, which are implemented by moving whole address chunks and splitting rows among the wire roles to shrink each recursive call.

quote.quote:
Its phase
frames express a $C$ tensor product using smaller groups of
selected bits, separated by binary changes of basis. We implement those
changes by moving whole address chunks. Splitting complete rows among
the network's wire roles then reduces the volume of each recursive
call. Finally, we bound the intermediate dyadic values and convert the
completed $C$ layer to the normalized $H_0$ layer. The entire layer is
evaluated exactly before one final truncation.

children.salient: The cost is $O(Vd^{\lambda'})$ for $d$ axes at once, strictly sublinear in the number of axes; it comes from the same strict inequality $s_{\rm c}/W_{\rm c}<m^\sigma$ that saves a power in address interchange.

adds.name: chunk count
adds.meaning: The maximum number of address chunks whose selected bits are butterflied at once.

adds.name: chunk width
adds.meaning: The number of address bits in each chunk.

adds.name: record length
adds.meaning: The number of complex coefficients in each polynomial record.

children.claim: With frames diagonalized by Hadamard matrices and phases $i^{\mathrm{wt}}$, the change across any edge is a product of translation kernels $C_v=aI+bX_v$, one per orthonormal basis vector of its residual, and $H_0^{\otimes D}=b^D\mathcal S_DC^{\otimes D}\mathcal S_D$.
children.method: Replace the shear frames of the bit network by phase frames $\mathcal C_U=H^{\otimes m}\operatorname{diag}(i^{q_U(x)})H^{\otimes m}$, so an edge change becomes kernels $C=H\mathsf SH=aI+bX$ on the residual directions, then return to the normalised butterfly through $H_0=b\mathsf SC\mathsf S$.

motivation.text: Hadamard conjugation turns the diagonal phases into translations, which are exactly two-point kernels, and the residual dimension counts how many such kernels an edge needs, matching the rank count of the bit network.

children.salient: All coefficients stay Gaussian dyadics ($\mathbb Z[i,1/2]$): the kernel $C$ has $C^2=X$ and $C^4=I$, and the plain butterfly $H_0$ is recovered from $C$ by diagonal fourth-root phases and a scalar $b^D$ that is only a shift and a phase.

children.claim: The complex network has total residual dimension $s_{\rm c}=W_{\rm c}m-2N+2L_{\rm c}<W_{\rm c}m$, and telescoping the phase frames gives $C^{\otimes m}$ on every role, scratch roles included.

quote.quote:
The sum of these basis lengths is
\[
 s_{\rm c}=W_{\rm c}m-2N+2L_{\rm c}
 =1873807244636671267308000000<W_{\rm c}m.

children.claim: For an edge from label $U_-$ to $U_+$ with orthonormal residual basis $v_1,\ldots,v_{\rho_{\rm edge}}$, the frame change is $\prod_j(aI+bX_{v_j})^{\epsilon_j}$ with $\epsilon_j=\pm1$.

quote.quote:
Proposition~\ref{prop:complex-motif-interface} gives the frame change
\[
 \mathcal C_{U_+}\mathcal C_{U_-}^{-1}
 =\prod_{j=1}^{\rho_{\rm edge}}(aI+bX_{v_j})^{\epsilon_j},
 \qquad \epsilon_j\in\{1,-1\}.

children.claim: Applying the network with these column frames to a group of $e=mf$ axes uses exactly $s_{\rm c}$ child calls, each on the $f=e/m$ axes of one slot.

quote.quote:
Summing its residual dimensions gives exactly
$s_{\rm c}$ child calls, each on the $f=e/m$ axes of one slot.

quote.quote:

$q=\lceil n/b\rceil$ nonnegative digits.  Their product has degree at most
\[
 2q-2<2n/b\le T/2<S.
\]

children.method: Use the Chinese-remainder (Agarwal–Cooley) map with coordinate powers $\mu_i$ chosen so that the new coordinate of axis $i$ depends only on lower-index digits, making the change of order triangular, then implement it by controlled cyclic shifts and axis exchanges.

children.claim: Each triangular update is a prefix-controlled cyclic shift: prepare the offset, split the valid target interval into two pieces and merge them in the opposite order.

quote.quote:

controls precede its target in the current physical order.  For each
prefix, prepare the offset, split the valid target interval into its
two consecutive pieces, and merge those pieces in the opposite order.

adds.name: margin
adds.meaning: The amount by which the power of p of the i-th dominant cost term falls below one.

children.claim: The margins are $g_1=1-\epsilon(1+c)$, $g_2=\epsilon c(1-\tau)$, $g_3=\epsilon(1-\lambda')$, $g_4=1-\tau-\epsilon(2-\tau)$, $g_5=1/4-\delta-3\epsilon/2$, $g_6=1-\delta-\epsilon$, $g_7=\epsilon$.

quote.quote:
g_1&=1-\epsilon(1+c),\qquad
 g_2=\epsilon c(1-\tau),\qquad
 g_3=\epsilon(1-\lambda'),\\
 g_4&=1-\tau-\epsilon(2-\tau),\qquad
 g_5=1/4-\delta-3\epsilon/2,\\
 g_6&=1-\delta-\epsilon,\qquad g_7=\epsilon.

Direct substitution gives
\[
 g_1>\frac12,\quad g_2=2^{-181},\quad g_3=2^{-129},\quad
 g_4>2^{-51},\quad g_5>\frac18,\quad g_6>\frac12,\quad g_7=2^{-75}.
\]

children.claim: Below a fixed cutoff use schoolbook multiplication; the single fixed-alphabet, fixed-tape deterministic machine then has worst-case time $O(n(\lg n)^{1-\kappa})$ for every input length and outputs the exact $2n$-bit product.

quote.quote:

conditions, and use schoolbook multiplication below it.  The finitely
many smaller lengths are included by enlarging the implicit constant.
With $\lg n=\max\{\lceil\log_2n\rceil,1\}$, the resulting single
fixed-alphabet, fixed-tape deterministic machine has worst-case time
$O(n(\lg n)^{1-\kappa})$ for every input length and produces precisely
the required $2n$-bit product.
